content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Technical Tutorial: Replication Strategies in System Design"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Data replication involves storing copies of the same data across multiple storage nodes to achieve high availability, low latency, and fault tolerance. Choosing the correct replication strategy is fundamental to distributed system design, directly impacting consistency, availability, and partition tolerance (CAP Theorem)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Leader-Follower Replication (Master-Slave)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"In Leader-Follower replication, one node is designated as the leader (primary) and all other replicas are followers (read replicas, secondaries). Clients send all write requests to the leader, which writes the data to its local storage and then sends a stream of data change events to all followers. Followers apply these changes in the exact same order."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Synchronous vs Asynchronous: Synchronous replication guarantees that the leader only acknowledges a write to the client after all followers confirm the write. This ensures strong consistency but reduces write availability and increases latency. Asynchronous replication returns success to the client immediately after the leader writes locally, trading consistency for high performance."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Read Scaling: Reads can be scaled horizontally by directing read queries to follower nodes, though this introduces potential read-after-write consistency issues if replication lags."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"Client Write -> Leader Node -> Propagates to Follower A & Follower B"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Multi-Leader Replication (Master-Master)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Multi-Leader replication extends the leader concept by allowing multiple nodes to accept write requests. Each leader acts as both a leader for its local clients and a follower for other leaders. This topology is particularly useful for multi-datacenter deployments where local writes are necessary to minimize network latency."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Write Conflict Resolution: The primary challenge in multi-leader setups is write conflicts. If two clients modify the same record concurrently on two different leaders, the changes must be resolved. Common strategies include Last Write Wins (LWW), conflict resolution code, or CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"Client A -> Leader 1 <---> Leader 2 <- Client B (Async Replication)"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Leaderless Replication (Dynamo-Style)"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Leaderless replication abandons the concept of a primary node entirely. In this architecture, clients write directly to multiple replicas, or a coordinator node forwards the write to several replicas. Because nodes can fail or lag, reading and writing rely on quorum systems to ensure consistency."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Quorum Reads and Writes: To guarantee up-to-date reads without a leader, the read and write operations must satisfy the formula: W + R > N, where N is the number of replicas, W is the minimum successful writes required, and R is the minimum successful reads required."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Anti-Entropy and Read Repair: When stale data is detected via version numbers or vector clocks, systems use Read Repair (updating stale replicas during a read) or Anti-Entropy background processes (background sync jobs) to synchronize data."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"Client Write -> Replica Node 1, Replica Node 2, Replica Node 3 (Simultaneous)"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Selection Criteria"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Leader-Follower for standard web applications requiring robust read scaling and simple transactional consistency."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Multi-Leader for globally distributed systems, collaborative editing tools, or offline-first applications."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Leaderless for high-availability systems that demand continuous uptime and can tolerate eventual consistency models."}]
